minors.title: spec.exec_ok reports 0.0 instead of null when every spec row's exec_ok is null (arm probe_nofill)
minors.detail: Pre-existing code the fix diff did not touch, so recorded as minor per the re-review protocol. _spec_block still computes exec_ok as _rate(float(spec["exec_ok"].sum()), n). I measured that Polars Series.sum() of an all-null Boolean column returns 0, not None, so an all-null exec_ok yields exec_ok = 0.0 rather than None. agent/inject.py's probe_nofill branch (around line 200) sets exec_ok = None on every spec row it writes, so a probe_nofill inject run reports spec.exec_ok = 0.0 in run_report.json and spec_exec_ok = 0.0 in done.json — a false "speculation never succeeded" where SCORE-2's own rule (null when there is no value) would give null. tool_agree and call_agree have the same shape on that arm, since gen_call is null on every row and both fall into the all-False branch. The SCORE-2 fix closed the .mean() family; this is the .sum() side of the same question, left for the final review, not a defect the fix introduced.

minors.title: the close-failure stderr line interpolates str(exc) only, so an exception with no message names nothing
minors.detail: The new line is `print(f"agent.loop: task {task_id} seed {seed}: env.close() failed: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)`. `str(exc)` is empty for an exception raised without arguments, so the operator gets a line that names the task and the seed but not the failure. Reproduced with the same fixture, raising `TimeoutError()` instead of `RuntimeError("world.close failed")` on the first triple: stderr is `agent.loop: task t_1 seed 42: env.close() failed:` and nothing else, while the finding asks for the exception to be named. The same function already has the convention that fits: the generic guard writes `abort=f"task_error:{type(exc).__name__}"`. `{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}` would name the exception in both cases. Diagnostic only -- the walk, the records and the heartbeat all behave correctly.

minors.title: the one launches builder is fed two different value shapes, and its docstring says the opposite
minors.detail: `_launch_entry` is shared, but its two callers hand it different types for the same two fields: launch() passes cards/cmd as {piece index: value} maps (lines 855, 857) while refire() passes bare strings (line 979). meta.json's append-only `launches` list therefore now holds heterogeneous entries - my run produced entry 0 with cards {'0': '', '1': '0', '2': ''} and a dict cmd, entry 1 with cards '' and a str cmd. Two statements assert the reverse: the builder's own docstring (line 675) says "so the two write one shape", and the report's self-review (T12-report.md:632-635) says refire now writes "a single-key {index: value} map where the old code wrote a bare string", which the code does not do. A second, smaller wrinkle in the same place: launch()'s maps are keyed by the integer piece index, so JSON round-trips them back as the strings '0', '1', '2', and a future reader joining on a piece's integer index finds nothing. Nothing reads launches[].cards or launches[].cmd on this branch today (the only reader is refire's `prior` count over `pieces`, which is a list of indices in both shapes and works), so this costs nothing at runtime - but the two docstring/report claims are wrong as written and should either be corrected or the shapes made to agree.

minors.title: registry._alive_on does not canonicalise the host it tests against failed_hosts, so it now disagrees with launch._piece_alive
minors.detail: Code the fix diff did not touch, recorded as minor per the protocol. `jobs/registry._alive_on` (line 518) tests `host in sessions.failed_hosts` on the raw host string, while the fixed `jobs/launch._piece_alive` canonicalises through the `hosts:` alias column first. failed_hosts is filled from host['name'] in live_sessions(), so a piece recorded under an alias never matches there: with failed_hosts={'tokyo105'} and a piece on host 'shiga', I measured registry._alive_on(...) == False against launch._piece_alive(...) == True on identical input. The launch.py side is the correct one; registry's own fail-closed test is the one that loses a piece on an unreachable aliased host (tokyo105/shiga and tokyo108/saitama are the two aliased entries in constants/path_outputs.yaml).
